question: Before moving off from a parked position, what should you do?
options: Signal first, then check your mirrors
Check your mirrors and blind spot, then signal if needed
Only check the interior mirror
Sound your horn to warn other traffic
explanation: Observe first — mirrors and a shoulder check for the blind spot — so your signal reflects what you've actually seen, then move off only when it's safe.

question: Why should you check your mirrors regularly while driving, not just before a manoeuvre?
options: To adjust your seating position
So you build an ongoing picture of what's happening around you
It's required by law every 10 seconds
To check your own appearance
explanation: Regular mirror checks keep you aware of following traffic, so nothing behind you comes as a surprise when you do need to slow down or turn.

question: You're using a hands-free phone kit while driving. What's true about this?
options: It's completely safe because your hands stay on the wheel
It can still reduce your concentration and slow your reactions
It's only risky in bad weather
It's only an offence if a police officer sees you holding the phone
explanation: The conversation itself divides your attention, not just where your hands are. The safest option is to let calls go to voicemail until you've stopped safely.

question: What should you do before setting off in a vehicle you're not familiar with?
options: Just start driving carefully
Adjust the seat, mirrors and head restraint before moving off
Only adjust the mirrors once you're already moving
Ask a passenger to sort out the mirrors for you
explanation: Getting your driving position right before you move off means you won't be fumbling with controls, or driving with a badly-placed head restraint, once you're in traffic.

question: Which of these is most likely to reduce your ability to concentrate while driving?
options: Keeping the cabin well ventilated
Driving when you're very tired
Planning your route before setting off
Keeping a safe distance from the vehicle in front
explanation: Fatigue slows reaction times and narrows attention in the same way as alcohol. If you're struggling to concentrate, that's a sign to stop and rest.

question: You're approaching a junction where parked vehicles block your view of the road you're joining. You should
options: edge forward slowly and carefully until you can see clearly
sound your horn and pull out anyway
accelerate quickly to get through the gap
flash your headlights to warn other traffic
explanation: A restricted view means you creep forward until you have a clear line of sight, rather than relying on sound or hoping other drivers give way.

question: You're about to change lanes on a dual carriageway. Before you signal, you should
options: check your mirrors and glance over your shoulder for the blind spot
just flick your indicator on
speed up so you can move across quickly
wait for the driver behind to flash their lights at you
explanation: Mirrors don't show everything — a following vehicle can sit just out of view in your blind spot, so a shoulder check confirms it's actually clear.

question: Loud music playing in your car while you drive can
options: help you stay alert
mask sounds like sirens or horns that warn you of hazards
improve your reaction times
have no real effect on your driving
explanation: You rely on hearing as well as sight to notice hazards — an approaching emergency vehicle or another driver's horn can be drowned out.

question: You feel your attention drifting on a long, straight motorway because you're bored. You should
options: speed up to reach your destination sooner
plan a break at the next safe opportunity, such as a services
open a window and carry on at the same speed
ignore it — boredom doesn't really affect driving
explanation: A drop in concentration is a warning sign in its own right. Stopping to rest, get some air and refocus is safer than pushing on.

question: What's the safest way to use a sat nav while driving?
options: Set your destination before you set off, and only glance at it briefly when it's safe to
Programme the destination while you're moving in slow traffic
Hold it in your hand so you can see it clearly
Watch it constantly so you don't miss a turn
explanation: Programming a device while driving — even in slow traffic — takes your eyes and attention off the road. Set it up before you move off.

question: Why is it important to check your mirrors well before you slow down or stop?
options: So you can identify the fastest lane
So you know how the traffic behind you will be affected
It isn't necessary if you're already going slowly
Only lorry drivers need to check behind before stopping
explanation: Braking without warning can catch a following driver out. Checking early lets you judge whether you need to signal your brake lights sooner, or brake more gently.

question: You keep glancing at texts arriving on your phone, propped in a holder, while driving. This is
options: fine, as long as the phone is in a proper holder
still a serious distraction, even though your hands are off the phone
only a problem if you reply to the texts
acceptable at low speeds
explanation: Reading a message pulls your eyes and mind off the road for several seconds — at 30mph that's many car lengths travelled without your full attention.

question: A vehicle behind you is following far too closely (tailgating). What should you do?
options: Brake sharply to warn them off
Increase your following distance from the vehicle ahead to give yourself more room to react
Speed up to get away from them
Signal and pull over immediately regardless of where you are
explanation: Opening up extra space ahead gives you a bigger safety margin, so you're not forced into a sudden stop that the tailgater has no time to react to.

question: At night, an oncoming vehicle is dazzling you with full-beam headlights. You should
options: flash your own full beam back at them
slow down and avoid looking directly at their lights
close your eyes briefly
speed up to pass them quickly
explanation: Looking slightly down and to the left of the road edge helps you keep your bearings without staring into the glare, while slowing down buys you more reaction time.

question: A learner driver ahead of you stalls at a junction. You should
options: sound your horn to hurry them along
be patient and give them time to move off safely
overtake them immediately
flash your headlights repeatedly
explanation: Everyone learns at some point. Pressuring a nervous driver increases the risk of a mistake — patience costs you a few seconds.

question: You hear a siren and see flashing blue lights approaching from behind. What should you do?
options: Stop immediately wherever you are, even in the middle of the junction
Look for a safe place to pull over and let the emergency vehicle pass, without breaking traffic laws to do so
Speed up to clear the way faster
Ignore it if you're not blocking the road
explanation: You should help emergency vehicles get through, but never by mounting a kerb, crossing a solid white line, or going through a red light — that just creates a new hazard.

question: Why should you dip your headlights when following another vehicle at night?
options: To save fuel
So your main beam doesn't dazzle the driver ahead through their mirrors
It's only necessary in towns
To make your car less visible
explanation: Full beam reflected in a mirror can dazzle the driver in front just as badly as an oncoming car's lights can dazzle you.

question: A cyclist is riding in the middle of a narrow lane ahead of you. This is likely because
options: they are being deliberately obstructive
the lane is too narrow for a car to safely overtake them, so they're preventing a dangerous squeeze
cyclists must always ride in the middle of the road
they haven't noticed you
explanation: Cyclists are advised to 'take the lane' where it's too narrow to overtake safely, precisely to stop drivers attempting a dangerous close pass.

question: Another driver makes a mistake and pulls out in front of you unexpectedly. What's the safest response?
options: React angrily by sounding your horn for a long period and flashing your lights
Stay calm, slow down if needed, and let it go
Overtake them aggressively to teach them a lesson
Tailgate them to show your frustration
explanation: Everyone makes mistakes occasionally. Reacting aggressively raises the risk for everyone involved and doesn't undo the error.

question: You're in slow-moving traffic and a driver from a side road wants to pull out just ahead of you. What should you do?
options: Speed up to close the gap so they can't get out
Consider letting them in if it's safe to do so
Sound your horn continuously
Never let another driver join your lane
explanation: Courteous driving keeps traffic flowing more smoothly for everyone and reduces frustration-driven mistakes.

question: You're overtaking a horse and rider on a country road. What should you do?
options: Pass as close as possible to save time
Sound your horn to let them know you're coming
Slow down, give them plenty of room, and pass wide and slow
Rev your engine so they know a car is near
explanation: Horses can startle at sudden noise or a close pass. Slowing down and giving generous space protects both the horse and rider.

question: Why is it bad practice to rev your engine or edge forward at a pedestrian crossing while someone is still crossing?
options: It saves you time
It can intimidate the pedestrian and put them at risk
It's a normal, courteous way to let them know you're waiting
It has no effect on the pedestrian
explanation: Pedestrians, especially children or elderly people, can be startled or feel pressured into hurrying, which increases the risk of a trip or misjudged step.

question: At a give-way junction, another driver flashes their headlights at you. This means
options: it is now definitely safe for you to proceed
they are only letting you know they're there — you must still make your own decision that it's safe
they are warning you to stop
you must always give way in response
explanation: A flashed headlight isn't an official signal with one fixed meaning. Always check for yourself before you act on it.

question: You're driving in a long queue of slow-moving traffic. What's good practice?
options: Keep changing lanes to find the fastest one
Stay patient, keep a safe gap, and avoid unnecessary lane changes
Use the hard shoulder to get ahead
Tailgate the vehicle in front so no one can cut in
explanation: Weaving between lanes in queueing traffic rarely saves real time and increases the risk of a low-speed collision.

question: How does the legal drink-drive limit in Scotland compare to the limit in England and Wales?
options: It's exactly the same
It's lower in Scotland, so less alcohol can put you over the limit
It's higher in Scotland
Scotland has no legal limit
explanation: England and Wales set the limit at 35 micrograms of alcohol per 100ml of breath (80mg per 100ml of blood); Scotland's limit is lower, at 22 micrograms per 100ml of breath (50mg per 100ml of blood). The only safe approach is not to drink at all if you're driving.

question: What is the legal minimum tread depth for a car tyre in the UK?
options: 1.0mm
1.6mm across the central three-quarters of the tread, all the way round
2.5mm
There is no legal minimum, only a recommendation
explanation: 1.6mm is the legal minimum across the central three-quarters of the tread width, around the entire circumference of the tyre.

question: Your dashboard shows a red warning light for engine oil pressure. What should you do?
options: Keep driving until you reach your destination
Stop as soon as it's safe to do so and check the situation before continuing
Turn the radio up and ignore it
Only worry if a second light also comes on
explanation: A red warning light generally means stop and investigate — continuing to drive with low oil pressure can cause serious engine damage.

question: Why is it important to keep your windscreen and windows clean?
options: It's only about appearance
Dirt and smears can restrict your view of hazards, especially in low sun
It has no effect on safety
Only the windscreen matters, side windows don't
explanation: A dirty windscreen scatters light from low sun or oncoming headlights, making it much harder to see clearly at exactly the moments you need to.

question: Leaving your engine running unnecessarily while parked (idling) mainly causes
options: improved fuel efficiency
unnecessary emissions and air pollution, especially in built-up areas
better engine performance
no real effect on anything
explanation: Switching off the engine when you're stationary for a while reduces exhaust emissions and local air pollution, particularly around schools and in town centres.

question: Who is legally responsible for making sure a child under 14 is wearing a seatbelt or is in an appropriate child restraint?
options: The child themselves
The driver of the vehicle
No one — it's only a recommendation for children
The vehicle's registered keeper, even if not present
explanation: The driver must make sure any passenger under 14 is correctly restrained before setting off.

question: Why should you check your tyre pressures regularly?
options: Under- or over-inflated tyres can affect grip, braking, fuel economy and tyre wear
It's only important before a long motorway journey
Tyre pressure has no effect on handling
Only front tyres need checking
explanation: Correct tyre pressure affects how much control and grip you have, as well as how quickly you can stop.

question: You notice your brakes feel spongy or the car pulls to one side when braking. What should you do?
options: Carry on driving as normal
Get the brakes checked by a qualified mechanic as soon as possible
Just brake more gently from now on
Only worry about it if it gets much worse
explanation: Changes in how your brakes feel can signal a genuine fault. Braking is safety-critical, so it needs checking promptly.

question: Which of these is most likely to reduce your fuel consumption and emissions?
options: Harsh acceleration and late braking
Anticipating the road ahead and easing off early instead of braking hard
Carrying unnecessary weight in the boot
Keeping tyres under-inflated
explanation: Smooth, anticipatory driving — reading the road ahead and easing off the accelerator early — uses less fuel than accelerating hard and braking late.

question: Before a long journey, which basic vehicle checks are sensible?
options: None — modern cars don't need checking
Fuel, oil, coolant, tyre condition/pressure and that all lights work
Just the fuel level
Only the windscreen wipers
explanation: A quick check of fluids, tyres and lights before setting off can catch a problem while you're still safely at home, rather than on the road.

question: The amber warning light for the anti-lock braking system (ABS) comes on and stays on while you're driving. This most likely indicates
options: everything is working perfectly
there may be a fault with the ABS system, and it should be checked
the car will not be able to brake at all
it only relates to the handbrake
explanation: An ABS warning light suggests the anti-lock system itself may not be working correctly, even though normal braking will usually still function — get it checked.

question: Why should you avoid leaving pets or children unattended in a parked vehicle on a warm day?
options: It's not actually a risk if the windows are cracked open
The temperature inside a car can rise very quickly and become dangerous
It's only a problem in direct sunlight
Modern cars don't heat up significantly
explanation: Car interiors can heat up rapidly even on a mild day, which can be extremely dangerous for anyone left inside, especially children and pets.

question: What is the purpose of a head restraint fitted correctly to your seat?
options: To improve comfort only
To reduce the risk of whiplash injury in a collision
It has no real safety function
To improve your view in the mirrors
explanation: A correctly adjusted head restraint — roughly level with the top of your head and close to it — helps limit how far your head snaps back in a rear-end collision.

question: In good, dry conditions, what following distance from the vehicle in front is generally recommended?
options: At least a 2-second gap
As close as possible to save space
Half a car length regardless of speed
There's no useful guideline
explanation: The 'two-second rule' gives you a simple way to judge a safe gap in good conditions — pick a fixed point and count how long it takes you to reach it after the car ahead passes it.

question: In wet weather, how should you adjust your following distance compared to dry conditions?
options: No change is needed
At least double it, since stopping distances increase
Halve it to keep traffic flowing
Only adjust your speed, not your distance
explanation: Wet roads reduce tyre grip, so your braking distance increases — doubling your gap gives you the extra room you'll need to stop safely.

question: On an icy road, stopping distances compared to a dry road can be
options: about the same
slightly less
up to ten times greater
impossible to estimate
explanation: Ice dramatically reduces tyre grip, and stopping distances can increase by a factor of up to ten — so a much bigger gap and gentler inputs are essential.

question: The overall stopping distance at 30mph in good conditions is typically around
options: 9 metres
23 metres (roughly 75 feet)
50 metres
96 metres
explanation: This is made up of thinking distance (around 9 metres) plus braking distance (around 14 metres), giving a total of about 23 metres.

question: The overall stopping distance at 70mph in good conditions is typically around
options: 23 metres
53 metres
96 metres (roughly 315 feet)
150 metres
explanation: At higher speeds both thinking distance and braking distance increase sharply — at 70mph the total is roughly four times the 30mph figure.

question: What is 'aquaplaning'?
options: A technique for cornering quickly
When a layer of water builds up between your tyres and the road, causing a loss of steering and braking control
A type of tyre designed for wet roads
Deliberately driving through puddles
explanation: If you start to aquaplane, ease off the accelerator gently and avoid braking or steering sharply until you feel the tyres regain grip.

question: Thinking distance — the distance travelled before you even start to brake — increases mainly because of
options: worn tyres
your speed and your reaction time (which is affected by tiredness, alcohol, drugs or distraction)
the weight of your vehicle
the colour of your car
explanation: Thinking distance depends on how fast you're travelling and how quickly you react — anything that slows your reactions increases it.

question: When towing a caravan or trailer, your overall stopping distance will typically
options: stay exactly the same
increase, due to the extra weight
decrease, due to extra stability
only change on motorways
explanation: Extra weight behind you increases the distance needed to stop safely, so extra following distance is needed too.

question: In foggy conditions, why should you increase your safety margin even further than for wet roads?
options: Fog doesn't actually affect stopping distances
Reduced visibility gives you less time to spot and react to hazards ahead
Fog only affects motorcyclists
It's only relevant at night
explanation: With visibility reduced, you may see a hazard much later than usual, so slowing down and increasing your gap gives you the time you'd otherwise lose.

question: Driving downhill, your vehicle tends to gain speed. What helps you keep a safe margin?
options: Coast in neutral to save fuel
Select a lower gear to use engine braking, in addition to the footbrake as needed
Ride the footbrake continuously all the way down
Increase speed to get down faster
explanation: Riding the brakes continuously can cause them to overheat and become less effective — using a lower gear helps control your speed more safely.

question: Crosswinds are strongest and most likely to affect your steering
options: only on motorways
when overtaking a high-sided vehicle or emerging from a sheltered area into open road
only when it's raining
they have no real effect on cars
explanation: A sudden gap in shelter — like passing a lorry or coming out from behind a hedge line — can expose you to a gust that pushes the vehicle sideways.

question: Why is it useful to leave a bigger gap to the vehicle in front when you're being followed closely by a tailgater?
options: It isn't useful, the gap in front makes no difference
It gives you more room to slow down gradually rather than braking sharply, reducing the tailgater's risk of hitting you
It encourages the tailgater to overtake dangerously
It's only relevant on single carriageways
explanation: A bigger cushion in front means you can ease off gradually instead of braking hard, giving a following driver who is too close more time to react.

question: What is a 'developing hazard'?
options: A hazard that has already caused a collision
Something that may require you to take action, such as slowing down or changing course, as it unfolds
Any parked vehicle, regardless of context
A hazard that only appears on motorways
explanation: A developing hazard is something you spot early and keep watching as it changes — for example a ball rolling into the road, which might be followed by a child.

question: You see a bus stopped ahead at a bus stop with its indicator on. What should you anticipate?
options: Nothing in particular
It may pull out, and pedestrians may cross from in front of or behind it
It will definitely stay stationary for a long time
Buses always have priority so you must stop immediately
explanation: A stopped bus can hide pedestrians who then step out around it, and the bus itself may indicate to pull away — both are worth watching for.

question: Which of these can seriously impair your ability to spot and react to hazards?
options: Wearing sunglasses on a bright day
Alcohol, drugs (including some over-the-counter or prescription medicines), tiredness and illness
Keeping both hands on the wheel
Using your mirrors regularly
explanation: All of these can slow your reactions and narrow your attention — always check medicine labels for warnings about driving.

question: You're approaching a parked car with steam or exhaust visible and its brake lights on. This suggests
options: nothing worth noting
the driver may be about to move off or open a door — be ready to react
the car is definitely abandoned
you should overtake immediately without slowing
explanation: Small clues like this are exactly what hazard perception training is about — reading signs that someone or something is about to move.

question: Why should you scan further ahead than just the vehicle directly in front of you?
options: It isn't necessary if you're keeping a safe distance
It gives you more time to notice a developing hazard and react smoothly
Only professional drivers need to do this
It's only useful in town centres
explanation: Looking well ahead — past the car in front, towards the next junction or brake lights further down the road — buys you valuable extra reaction time.

question: You notice a line of parked cars ahead with a gap between two of them. What should you consider?
options: Nothing, gaps between parked cars are irrelevant
A pedestrian, especially a child, could step out from the gap without warning
You should speed up to pass the gap quickly
Only cyclists use gaps like this
explanation: Gaps in parked vehicles are a classic place for a pedestrian to emerge suddenly, often partly hidden until the last moment.

question: What effect does tiredness have on hazard perception?
options: None, as long as you're an experienced driver
It slows your reactions and can cause you to miss developing hazards altogether
It only affects night driving
It sharpens your focus
explanation: A tired driver can experience 'microsleeps' — brief lapses of attention lasting only a second or two — which is more than enough time to miss a hazard.

question: Approaching a roundabout, why is it useful to identify your exit early?
options: It isn't useful — just follow the car in front
It helps you choose the correct lane in good time and signal appropriately
You should always take the first exit regardless
Roundabouts don't require planning ahead
explanation: Deciding your exit early lets you position your vehicle correctly and signal in good time, rather than swerving lanes at the last moment.

question: You see brake lights come on several vehicles ahead of you, even though the car directly in front hasn't braked yet. What should you do?
options: Ignore it since your car in front hasn't reacted
Start easing off the accelerator in anticipation, since the hazard is likely to reach you too
Speed up to see what's happening
Wait until the car directly ahead brakes before reacting
explanation: Reading hazards further down the road, not just the vehicle immediately ahead, lets you respond smoothly instead of reacting late.

question: Which of these is a 'potential hazard' that hasn't yet become a developing one?
options: A child already running into the road
A ball lying still on a pavement near a park, with no one visible nearby yet
A car that has just braked hard in front of you
A pedestrian already stepping off the kerb
explanation: Spotting a potential hazard early — before it starts to develop — means you're already prepared if it does turn into something you need to react to.

question: Why might driving through a residential area with parked cars on both sides require extra caution?
options: It never requires extra caution
Reduced visibility and the chance of a pedestrian, cyclist or car door appearing suddenly between vehicles
Residential roads always have a 20mph limit, which removes any risk
Parked cars have no effect on hazard awareness
explanation: Narrow gaps between parked cars can hide pedestrians and restrict your view, so a lower speed and extra vigilance are appropriate.

question: What is the main purpose of the hazard perception element of the theory test?
options: To test how fast you can react to a loud noise
To check you can spot developing hazards in good time, as you would need to in real driving
To test your knowledge of road signs
To assess your parking ability
explanation: It's designed to reflect a core real-world skill: noticing a hazard early enough that you have time to respond calmly, not just quickly.

question: A pedestrian has stepped onto a zebra crossing. What must you do?
options: Continue if you have priority as the vehicle
Stop and allow them to cross — pedestrians have priority once they've stepped onto a zebra crossing
Sound your horn and proceed slowly
Only stop if there's more than one pedestrian
explanation: Once someone has stepped onto a zebra crossing, they have priority and you must stop and wait for them to finish crossing.

question: You're overtaking a cyclist on a 30mph road. How much space should you generally aim to leave?
options: No specific space is needed if you're going slowly
As much space as you would leave for a car — at least about 1.5 metres where possible
You should not overtake cyclists at all
Just enough that your mirror doesn't hit them
explanation: Cyclists can wobble or need to avoid drain covers and debris — giving generous space (and slowing down if you can't) keeps everyone safer.

question: A school crossing patrol ('lollipop person') has stepped into the road and is displaying their sign. You must
options: stop and wait until the sign is withdrawn and the crossing is clear
proceed carefully if no children are visible
sound your horn to move them along
only stop if you can see children waiting
explanation: The sign is a clear instruction to stop — you must wait until it's withdrawn, even if you can't immediately see why.

question: Why should you take extra care near horse riders?
options: Horses are unaffected by traffic noise
Horses can be easily startled by sudden noise or a close, fast-moving vehicle, which is dangerous for horse and rider
It's only a concern on motorways, where horses are common
There's no need for extra care once you've passed
explanation: Passing slowly and leaving plenty of room reduces the chance of startling the horse, which could unseat the rider or cause it to bolt into traffic.

question: At a junction, why should you take particular care to check for motorcyclists before pulling out?
options: Motorcycles are easier to see than cars
Their narrower profile can make them easy to miss or misjudge for distance and speed
Motorcyclists always have less priority than cars
It's only a concern at night
explanation: A motorcycle's smaller size can make it harder to judge how far away it is and how fast it's approaching — a careful second look helps.

question: You see a driver displaying a green 'P' plate. This usually means
options: the vehicle is a taxi
the driver has recently passed their test and may still be building experience and confidence
the driver is exempt from speed limits
the vehicle is being used for a driving lesson
explanation: Green P plates are a voluntary way for newly qualified drivers to signal this to others — a little extra patience and space is appreciated.

question: Why might elderly or disabled pedestrians need more time to cross a road?
options: They don't — everyone crosses at the same speed
They may walk more slowly or have reduced awareness of approaching traffic, so may need longer and more obvious care from drivers
Only wheelchair users need extra time
Traffic signals already account for this automatically everywhere
explanation: Being ready to wait a little longer, without rushing or edging forward, helps pedestrians who may move more slowly or less predictably.

question: Children are playing near the pavement as you approach in your car. What should you do?
options: Maintain your speed since they are on the pavement, not the road
Slow down and be prepared for a child to run into the road unexpectedly
Sound your horn to warn them off
Speed up to pass the area quickly
explanation: Children can be unpredictable and may not judge traffic speed accurately, so slowing down gives you time to react if one runs out.

question: What does the 'hierarchy of road users' principle mean in practice?
options: Pedestrians must always give way to vehicles
Those who can do the greatest harm to others (like drivers of large or fast vehicles) have the greatest responsibility to reduce the danger they pose to more vulnerable road users
It only applies to cyclists
It has no real effect on how anyone should behave
explanation: The idea is that responsibility for safety increases with the potential to cause harm — so drivers and larger vehicles are expected to take the most care around pedestrians and cyclists.

question: You're approaching a 'pelican' crossing (a pedestrian crossing controlled by traffic lights, with no green man / red man figure) showing a flashing amber signal to you. This means
options: stop completely regardless of pedestrians
you may proceed if the crossing is clear of pedestrians, but must give way to anyone still crossing
the crossing is out of use
you must always stop, even if empty
explanation: A flashing amber phase allows traffic to move on if the crossing is clear, but pedestrians already crossing still have priority. Newer 'puffin' crossings work differently — they hold a steady red until sensors detect the crossing is clear, with no flashing amber phase.

question: Why is it important to check for cyclists before opening your car door after parking?
options: It isn't important — cyclists should watch for doors
A cyclist passing close to parked cars could be struck by a suddenly opened door ('dooring')
Cyclists never ride near parked cars
This only matters for the driver's door, not passengers'
explanation: Checking your mirror and looking back before opening any door — sometimes called the 'Dutch reach' when using the far hand — helps you spot an approaching cyclist in time.

question: A pedestrian with a long white cane and a red band is waiting to cross. What does this indicate?
options: Nothing specific
The person is deaf-blind, and may need extra time and space to cross safely
They are a road worker
It indicates a general mobility aid with no specific meaning
explanation: A white cane with a red band or reflective bands typically indicates the person is deaf-blind — extra patience and care are especially important.

question: Your rear wheels begin to skid on a bend. What is generally the correct response?
options: Brake hard immediately
Ease off the accelerator gently and steer smoothly to correct the skid, avoiding harsh braking
Accelerate to power out of it
Turn the wheel sharply in the opposite direction
explanation: Harsh braking or sudden steering can make a skid worse. Easing off and steering smoothly gives the tyres the best chance to regain grip.

question: In heavy rain, why might your vehicle be harder to control at higher speeds?
options: It wouldn't be — rain has no effect at speed
The risk of aquaplaning (losing contact with the road due to water) increases with speed
Rain only affects braking, not steering
Modern tyres are unaffected by water at any speed
explanation: As speed increases, tyres have less time to displace water from under them, raising the risk of aquaplaning and reduced steering/braking control.

question: When using anti-lock brakes (ABS) in an emergency stop, you should
options: pump the brake pedal rapidly yourself
apply firm, continuous pressure to the brake pedal and let the system do the pulsing
brake very lightly to avoid activating it
only use the handbrake
explanation: ABS is designed to prevent wheel lock-up on its own — firm, steady pressure lets it work as intended, rather than you trying to replicate its pumping action manually.

question: Driving down a long, steep hill, what technique helps you control your speed without overheating the brakes?
options: Coast in neutral the whole way down
Select a lower gear so engine braking helps control your speed
Ride the footbrake continuously
Switch off the engine to save fuel
explanation: Continuous heavy braking can cause the brakes to overheat and fade. Using a lower gear lets engine braking share the load.

question: In fog, why is it recommended to use dipped headlights rather than sidelights alone?
options: Dipped headlights make no real difference in fog
Dipped headlights make you more visible to other road users in poor visibility
Sidelights are always brighter than dipped headlights
It's only relevant during daylight fog
explanation: Being seen is just as important as seeing in fog — dipped headlights (and fog lights if visibility is seriously reduced) help other drivers spot you.

question: You're driving on a snow-covered road. Which of these helps maintain control?
options: Accelerating and braking harshly to break through the snow
Using gentle, smooth inputs on the accelerator, brakes and steering, and pulling away in a higher gear than usual
Driving at your normal speed as if the road were dry
Keeping the wheels spinning to generate heat and melt the snow
explanation: Smooth, gentle inputs reduce the chance of the wheels losing grip, and pulling away in a higher gear helps avoid wheelspin.

question: At night on an unlit road with no other traffic nearby, you should generally use
options: sidelights only
main (full) beam headlights, dipping them when you see an oncoming vehicle or one you're following
hazard warning lights
no lights at all to save the battery
explanation: Full beam gives you the best view of an unlit road, but must be dipped in good time to avoid dazzling oncoming or leading traffic.

question: Why should you slow down before entering a bend, rather than braking while turning?
options: It makes no real difference to grip
Braking while turning can upset the car's balance and reduce tyre grip, increasing the risk of a skid
You should always brake mid-corner for better control
It only matters for motorcycles
explanation: Slowing to the right speed before the bend, then gently accelerating through it, keeps the car's weight balanced and the tyres gripping well.

question: Strong, gusty winds are most likely to affect vehicle control when
options: driving on a motorway in still air
passing high-sided vehicles, bridges or gaps in hedges/buildings where a sudden gust can hit you
parked with the engine off
driving very slowly in a car park
explanation: A sudden gust after being sheltered can push the vehicle sideways with little warning — a firm, steady grip on the wheel helps you correct it.

question: What is 'engine braking'?
options: Using the handbrake instead of the footbrake
Using a lower gear to help slow the vehicle, reducing reliance on the footbrake alone
A fault where the engine won't start
Braking that only works when the engine is off
explanation: Selecting a lower gear increases resistance from the engine, which helps control speed, particularly useful on long descents.

question: Driving through a flooded section of road, what's good practice?
options: Drive through as fast as possible to get through quickly
Drive slowly in a low gear, keeping the engine revs up slightly, then test your brakes gently once through
Stop in the middle of the flood to assess it
Switch off the engine while driving through
explanation: Slow, steady progress reduces the risk of water entering the engine, and testing your brakes afterwards helps dry them out and confirms they still work.

question: Why might a vehicle with worn shock absorbers be harder to control?
options: Worn shock absorbers have no effect on handling
The tyres can lose consistent contact with the road surface, reducing grip and increasing stopping distance
They only affect ride comfort, not safety
They mainly affect fuel economy
explanation: Shock absorbers help keep tyres pressed firmly onto the road — when worn, the car can bounce more after bumps, briefly reducing grip.

question: When joining a motorway from a slip road, you should
options: stop at the end of the slip road and wait for a gap
match your speed to the traffic already on the motorway and merge when it's safe
always have priority over traffic already on the motorway
join at a much lower speed than the traffic flow, regardless of conditions
explanation: Traffic already on the motorway has priority — using the slip road to build up to a similar speed lets you merge smoothly rather than forcing your way in.

question: On a three-lane motorway in normal conditions, which lane should you normally drive in unless overtaking?
options: Whichever lane you like at all times
The left-hand lane, moving out to overtake and then returning left when it's safe
The middle lane, to avoid slower traffic
The right-hand lane, for the fastest progress
explanation: 'Middle-lane hogging' — sitting in the middle lane without overtaking — can be treated as careless driving; the left lane is the default unless you're passing slower traffic.

question: What is the hard shoulder on a traditional motorway primarily for?
options: Overtaking slower traffic
Emergency stops and breakdowns only
Undertaking in heavy traffic
General use during rush hour
explanation: The hard shoulder is reserved for genuine emergencies and breakdowns — using it for anything else is both dangerous and against the rules.

question: Can learner drivers drive on a motorway in Great Britain?
options: No, this is never permitted
Yes, but only when accompanied by an approved driving instructor in a car fitted with dual controls, and L plates displayed
Yes, completely unsupervised once they've had 10 lessons
Only at night
explanation: Learners are permitted on motorways specifically with an approved instructor in a dual-control vehicle. It's optional, not a required part of learning to drive — motorway driving isn't tested during the practical test itself.

question: A red 'X' symbol shown above a motorway lane on an overhead gantry means
options: overtaking is encouraged in that lane
the lane is closed — you must not drive in it
reduce speed to 30mph in that lane only
the lane is for emergency vehicles only, but others may use it if empty
explanation: A red X closes that lane completely, often because of an incident or maintenance ahead — moving in promptly and safely is important.

question: You want to leave the motorway at the next exit. What's good practice?
options: Cut across all lanes at the last moment
Move into the left-hand lane in good time, following the exit signs and markers
Slow down in the right-hand lane and wait for a gap
Use the hard shoulder to overtake and reach the exit
explanation: Positioning yourself in the left lane well before your exit avoids a last-minute, riskier lane change across multiple lanes.

question: In a motorway contraflow system, what should you expect?
options: Normal lane widths and no speed restrictions
Narrower lanes than usual and often a reduced, enforced speed limit
No change from normal motorway driving
Traffic will always be diverted off the motorway entirely
explanation: Contraflows usually mean narrower lanes shared closer to oncoming traffic, so a lower speed limit and extra concentration are needed.

question: What does a plain blue circular sign showing a white number (for example '40') mean, on the stretch of road where it applies?
options: A recommended maximum speed
A minimum speed limit which all traffic on that stretch must observe
A distance marker only
Advisory information with no legal force
explanation: Blue circular signs give a mandatory instruction — in this case, a minimum speed that must be maintained (commonly seen in tunnels), rather than a maximum. A matching sign with a red diagonal stripe marks the end of that minimum.

question: If your vehicle breaks down on a motorway and you can reach the hard shoulder, what should you do once stopped?
options: Stay in the vehicle with your seatbelt on
Get out and wait behind the barrier if possible, away from the carriageway and your vehicle
Stand behind your vehicle to warn other traffic
Attempt roadside repairs on the hard shoulder
explanation: Vehicles on the hard shoulder are at real risk of being struck — getting behind the barrier, away from moving traffic, is much safer than staying in or near the car.

question: Why should you avoid using a warning triangle on a motorway?
options: It's unnecessary because motorways never have hazards
Walking onto the carriageway to place one is dangerous given the speed of traffic
Warning triangles are illegal everywhere in the UK
They're only for use on roundabouts
explanation: The risk of being struck while placing a triangle on a high-speed road outweighs any benefit — use your hazard lights instead and get well clear of the carriageway.

question: What should you do if you feel sleepy while driving on a motorway?
options: Open a window and keep driving at the same speed
Leave at the next exit or services and take a proper break, rather than trying to push through
Increase your speed to reach your destination and rest sooner
Turn the radio up loudly
explanation: Fresh air and loud music only mask tiredness briefly — a real break, and ideally some sleep, is the only effective fix.

question: On motorways, what is 'undertaking' generally understood to mean, and why is caution needed?
options: Driving underneath a bridge
Overtaking on the left rather than the right — other drivers may not expect it, so extra care is needed
Following another vehicle too closely
Driving below the speed limit
explanation: Passing on the inside can catch other drivers by surprise since they're generally watching for overtaking traffic on their right.

question: What is the national speed limit for cars on a single carriageway road (where no other limit is signed)?
options: 50mph
60mph
70mph
40mph
explanation: Unless a lower limit is signed, the national speed limit for cars on a single carriageway is 60mph.

question: At a roundabout, unless signs or markings indicate otherwise, you should generally give way to
options: traffic approaching from your left
traffic already on the roundabout, approaching from your right
pedestrians only
no one, as you have priority once you enter
explanation: In the UK, traffic moves clockwise around roundabouts, so you generally give way to vehicles already on the roundabout coming from your right.

question: At an unmarked crossroads with no signs, road markings or signals, what applies?
options: The vehicle on the wider road always has priority
No one has automatic priority — proceed with caution and be ready to give way
The vehicle that arrives first always has priority
You must always give way to traffic from the right, by law
explanation: With no signs or markings, there's no automatic right of way — extra caution and clear observation are needed from everyone approaching.

question: You want to proceed straight ahead through a yellow box junction, but traffic ahead of you is stationary. What should you do?
options: Enter the box anyway since you have a green light
Wait until you can see your exit is clear before entering the box
Enter the box and stop inside it if necessary
Reverse to let other traffic go first
explanation: You must not enter a box junction unless your exit is clear — this prevents the junction from becoming gridlocked.

question: When may you enter a yellow box junction to turn right, even if your exit isn't fully clear?
options: Never, under any circumstances
If you're only prevented from proceeding by oncoming traffic, or by other vehicles also waiting to turn right
Any time you're turning right
Only late at night
explanation: This specific exception exists so right-turning traffic isn't permanently blocked while waiting for a gap in oncoming traffic.

question: Amber traffic lights on their own (not combined with red) mean
options: go, if the way is clear
stop, unless you've already crossed the stop line or stopping would be unsafe
speed up to clear the junction
the lights are broken and can be ignored
explanation: Amber alone is an instruction to stop, with the narrow exception of when you're already too far into the junction to stop safely.

question: Red and amber shown together at a traffic light mean
options: you may go immediately
prepare to move off, but you must still wait for green
stop and switch off your engine
the crossing is now closed to pedestrians only
explanation: This combination is a 'get ready' signal — green is still required before you actually move off.

question: Which of these generally indicates you must not park?
options: A single broken white line in the centre of the road
Double yellow lines along the edge of the road
A speed limit sign
A give way sign
explanation: Double yellow lines mean no waiting at any time, unless a nearby sign states otherwise (for example, seasonal restrictions or specific loading exceptions).

question: You're approaching a level crossing. A steady amber light shows, followed by flashing red lights. What should you do?
options: Speed up to cross before the barriers close
Stop, unless you've already crossed the stop line or it would be unsafe to stop
Ignore it if you can't see a train
Reverse away from the crossing
explanation: Level crossing signals must be obeyed just like traffic lights — the flashing red lights mean a train is approaching and you must not cross.

question: On a narrow road with passing places, and an oncoming vehicle approaches, what should you do?
options: Always force the other vehicle to reverse
Pull into a passing place, or wait opposite one, to let the oncoming vehicle pass
Drive through the middle of the road at speed
Flash your lights and continue at the same speed
explanation: Using passing places courteously — pulling in yourself, or stopping opposite one so the other driver can pull in — keeps narrow roads moving safely.

question: You're driving alongside a double white line system where the line nearest to you is solid. What does this generally mean?
options: You may cross it to overtake if the road is clear
You must not cross or straddle it, except in specific permitted situations such as entering a driveway or passing a stationary vehicle
It only applies to lorries
It's purely decorative and has no legal meaning
explanation: A solid line on your side generally prohibits overtaking or crossing, because it usually marks a stretch with limited visibility ahead. Permitted exceptions include entering a side road or driveway, passing a stationary vehicle, or overtaking a cyclist, horse or slow-moving road maintenance vehicle.

question: In a one-way street with two or more lanes, how do you know which lane to use for your destination?
options: Any lane can be used regardless of direction
Road markings and signs will indicate which lane to use depending on whether you're turning or going straight ahead
You should always use the rightmost lane
One-way streets never have more than one lane
explanation: Multi-lane one-way streets rely on lane markings and arrows to keep traffic flowing safely — position early according to where you plan to go.

question: What is the national speed limit for an ordinary car (not towing a trailer) on a dual carriageway or motorway?
options: 50mph
60mph
70mph
80mph
explanation: Unless a lower limit is signed, the national speed limit for cars and motorcycles on a dual carriageway or motorway is 70mph. Towing a trailer or caravan lowers this to 60mph on a dual carriageway/motorway and 50mph on a single carriageway.

question: What shape are most warning signs (alerting you to a hazard ahead) in the UK?
options: Circular
Triangular, with a red border
Rectangular
Octagonal
explanation: Triangular signs with a red border are used to warn of a hazard ahead, such as a bend, junction or crossing.

question: What shape is used uniquely for the 'STOP' sign, and why does this matter?
options: Circular, the same as other mandatory signs
Octagonal — its distinctive shape means it can be recognised even if obscured, e.g. by mud or snow
Triangular, same as warning signs
Rectangular
explanation: The STOP sign's unique eight-sided shape means drivers can often recognise it from its outline alone, even from behind or when partly covered.

question: Circular signs with a red border generally indicate
options: general information
a mandatory instruction or a prohibition — something you must or must not do
a warning of a hazard ahead
a direction to a tourist attraction
explanation: Red circles are used for orders — either telling you to do something specific or prohibiting an action, like 'no entry' or a speed limit.

question: Blue circular signs (without a red border) generally indicate
options: a warning
a positive instruction — something you must do, such as a mandatory direction or minimum speed
a prohibition
tourist information only
explanation: Blue circles give positive instructions, such as 'turn left ahead' or a minimum speed, rather than prohibiting something.

question: A plain white circular sign with a single black diagonal stripe across it, and no number, generally means
options: national speed limit applies
no entry for vehicles
give way ahead
no stopping at any time
explanation: This sign indicates the national speed limit applies for that type of road — 60mph on a single carriageway or 70mph on a dual carriageway/motorway for an ordinary car, unless a lower limit is otherwise signed.

question: What does a triangular sign showing two children walking mean?
options: School crossing patrol ahead only
Warning of a school entrance or area where children are likely to be crossing
No children allowed on this road
A playground is located here for information only
explanation: This warns drivers to be ready for children crossing, especially near school opening and closing times.

question: Rectangular road signs are typically used to give
options: warnings of hazards
information, such as directions or facilities available
mandatory instructions only
prohibitions only
explanation: Rectangular signs are generally informational, for example direction signs, place names, or notices about parking and facilities.

question: What does a solid white line along the centre of the road, running alongside a broken white line closer to you, mean?
options: You may overtake when it's safe, since the broken line is on your side
Neither vehicle may cross the line under any circumstances
It has no specific meaning
Only applies to buses and lorries
explanation: When the broken line is on your side, you may cross to overtake if it's safe and you can complete the manoeuvre before reaching any solid section on your side; the solid line on the other side is a legal prohibition on crossing from their direction, not just advice.

question: Yellow criss-cross diagonal lines painted on the road surface at a junction indicate
options: a pedestrian-only zone
a box junction — do not enter the marked area unless your exit is clear
a bus lane
a level crossing
explanation: This is the yellow box junction marking, designed to keep the junction clear so cross traffic isn't blocked.

question: What does a sign showing a red circle around the number 30 typically mean?
options: A recommended speed of 30mph
A maximum speed limit of 30mph that must not be exceeded
A minimum speed of 30mph
Distance to the next town is 30 miles
explanation: A red circle with a number is a mandatory maximum speed limit, not just a suggestion.

question: A triangular sign showing two straight arrows, one pointing up and one pointing down, warns of
options: a roundabout ahead
a two-way traffic system, for example where traffic normally flows one-way but changes to two-way ahead
a dual carriageway ending
road works ahead only
explanation: This sign warns that you're approaching a section where traffic flows in both directions, which may be unexpected after a one-way stretch.

question: What does a red-ringed circular sign showing a car and a motorcycle in black mean?
options: Cars and motorcycles have priority here
No motor vehicles are allowed beyond this point, not just cars and motorcycles
Parking permitted for cars and motorcycles only
A car and motorcycle dealership ahead
explanation: This sign prohibits motor vehicles generally — cars and motorcycles are shown as examples, but the restriction covers all motor vehicles, including vans, lorries and buses.

question: As a learner driver, who is permitted to supervise you while you practise in a car (outside of professional lessons)?
options: Anyone with a full driving licence, regardless of experience
Someone aged 21 or over who has held a full licence for the category of vehicle for at least 3 years
Any adult family member
Only a qualified driving instructor
explanation: Supervising drivers must meet both an age requirement and a minimum time holding a full licence for that vehicle category.

question: In Great Britain, a car first registered new needs its first MOT test
options: after 1 year
after 3 years, and then annually
after 5 years
MOT tests are not required for private cars
explanation: In Great Britain, cars and motorcycles generally need their first MOT once they reach 3 years old, and then every year after that. (Northern Ireland's rules differ slightly — first MOT at 4 years.)

question: What is the minimum level of motor insurance legally required to drive on public roads?
options: No insurance is required if you drive carefully
At least third-party cover
Fully comprehensive cover only
Third-party fire and theft is the legal minimum
explanation: Third-party insurance is the legal minimum — it covers damage or injury you cause to others, though it doesn't cover your own vehicle.

question: The V5C document for a vehicle is commonly known as the
options: MOT certificate
logbook — it shows the registered keeper details
insurance certificate
driving licence
explanation: The V5C shows who is registered as the keeper of the vehicle. It should be updated whenever the registered keeper changes.

question: What is the eyesight standard you must meet to drive, in simple terms?
options: Being able to read a car number plate from 20 metres away (with glasses or contact lenses if you normally wear them)
Having perfect eyesight with no aids of any kind
Only needing to see clearly in daylight
There is no formal minimum standard
explanation: If you can't meet this standard, even with glasses or contact lenses, you must not drive until it's corrected.

question: Under the 'new driver' rules, what happens if you build up 6 or more penalty points from offences committed within 2 years of passing your first practical test?
options: Nothing changes — the points simply stay on your licence
Your licence is revoked and you must reapply for a provisional licence and retake both theory and practical tests
You receive a formal warning letter only
You must attend a single awareness course and nothing else
explanation: This stricter rule for new drivers reflects that early driving experience carries higher risk — it effectively resets you to learner status. Points from an offence committed before you passed (for example, while a learner) can still count if they're given after you pass.

question: Vehicle Excise Duty is more commonly known as
options: road tax / car tax
MOT fee
congestion charge
insurance premium
explanation: Vehicle Excise Duty (VED) is the official name for what most people call road tax or car tax, and it's normally required to keep a vehicle on public roads.

question: What must L plates (or D plates in Wales) show, and where must they be displayed?
options: They are optional for confident learners
They must be clearly displayed on the front and back of the vehicle whenever a learner is driving
Only on the rear of the vehicle
Only required during driving lessons with an instructor
explanation: L plates must be visible on both the front and back of the car at all times a learner driver is at the wheel, not just during formal lessons.

question: If you're stopped by police and can't produce your licence, insurance and MOT certificate immediately, what usually happens?
options: You will always be prosecuted immediately with no alternative
You're usually given a set number of days to produce the documents at a police station
There is no requirement to ever show these documents
Your vehicle is automatically impounded on the spot
explanation: Police commonly issue a produce document requirement, giving you a short period to bring the documents to a police station if you don't have them on you.

question: Which type of insurance cover typically pays for damage to your own car, even if the accident was your fault?
options: Third party only
Third party, fire and theft
Comprehensive
None — no policy covers your own fault accidents
explanation: Comprehensive cover generally includes damage to your own vehicle as well as third-party liability, unlike third-party-only policies.

question: Why is it important to tell your insurer about modifications made to your car?
options: It isn't necessary if the modification is minor
Undisclosed modifications can invalidate your insurance policy
Insurers don't need to know about any vehicle changes
It only matters for commercial vehicles
explanation: Insurance is based on the risk profile they were told about — undeclared changes can mean a claim is refused later.

question: As a provisional licence holder, which of these must you also arrange before driving on the road?
options: Nothing extra, a provisional licence alone is sufficient
Valid insurance that covers you to drive, and display of L plates
A full driving test booking
Written permission from the DVSA
explanation: You need appropriate insurance cover (your own learner policy, or being covered on someone else's) as well as L plates displayed, in addition to holding a provisional licence.

question: You are the first to arrive at the scene of a collision. What is generally the first priority?
options: Move the injured people out of their vehicles immediately
Make the area safe — for example using hazard lights — before approaching, and check for danger before helping
Take photos before doing anything else
Leave immediately to avoid being involved
explanation: Protecting yourself and others from further danger — such as oncoming traffic or fire risk — comes before anything else, including trying to help casualties.

question: At the scene of a road traffic incident, when should you move an injured person from their vehicle?
options: As quickly as possible in every case
Generally, only if they are in immediate danger, such as from fire — otherwise avoid moving them in case of injuries like a spinal injury
Only if they ask to be moved
It's never appropriate to consider moving anyone
explanation: Moving someone with a potential spinal injury can cause serious harm — leave them where they are unless there's an immediate danger like fire.

question: The basic first steps often remembered as 'DR ABC' when approaching a casualty stand for
options: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation
Drive, Reverse, Assess, Brake, Call
Danger, Report, Ambulance, Bandage, Check
Distance, Response, Alert, Brace, Call
explanation: This memory aid guides a basic first-aid check: check for danger, check the casualty's response, then their airway, breathing and circulation.

question: You're involved in a minor collision with a parked, unattended vehicle and cause damage. What must you do?
options: Drive away, since no one witnessed it
Try to find the owner, or leave your name and contact details, and report it to the police within 24 hours if you can't
Only report it if the damage looks expensive
Nothing is required if it's a very minor scrape
explanation: You're legally required to try to inform the owner, and if that's not possible, you must report the incident to the police within 24 hours.

question: If your vehicle catches fire while driving, what should you do first?
options: Keep driving to the nearest garage
Stop as soon as safely possible, switch off the engine and get everyone well away from the vehicle
Open all the windows and continue
Try to extinguish it while still driving
explanation: A vehicle fire can spread very quickly — getting people a safe distance away is far more important than trying to save the vehicle.

question: You break down on a motorway and can't reach the hard shoulder or an emergency refuge area. What should you do?
options: Try to push the vehicle to safety yourself
Keep your hazard lights on, stay in the vehicle with your seatbelt on if you can't get out safely, and call for help
Leave the vehicle and walk along the live lane to get help
Attempt to reverse to the previous exit
explanation: If you can't get out of the vehicle safely, staying belted in with hazards on and calling for help (999 in a genuine emergency) is safer than stepping into a live lane.

question: At a motorway incident, roadside emergency telephones connect you to
options: a local taxi firm
the police or the relevant highways control centre, who can pinpoint your location automatically
a random call centre with no location information
your own vehicle breakdown provider only
explanation: Roadside emergency phones are linked to a control centre that can identify your exact location, which is especially useful in poor visibility or at night.

question: Why should you generally avoid removing a motorcyclist's helmet after a crash, unless absolutely necessary?
options: Helmets are not relevant to first aid
Incorrect removal can risk further injury, particularly to the neck or spine
It's always fine to remove it immediately
Only paramedics are allowed to touch a helmet, by law
explanation: Unless it's essential (for example, to help with breathing), leave helmet removal to trained paramedics who can do it safely.

question: You keep a basic first aid kit and warning triangle in your car. On which type of road is it best to avoid using the warning triangle?
options: A quiet residential street
A motorway, due to the danger of walking on or near a high-speed carriageway
A single carriageway A-road
It's safe to use anywhere without exception
explanation: On motorways, the risk of being struck while placing a triangle outweighs the benefit — rely on hazard lights instead and keep people well away from traffic.

question: If someone is not breathing and unresponsive after a collision, and you're trained to do so, what should you consider doing while waiting for the emergency services?
options: Nothing, wait for paramedics without acting
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), if you have appropriate training or are guided by the emergency call handler
Give them food or water
Move them into the recovery position immediately regardless of the situation
explanation: CPR can be critical in the first minutes — a 999 call handler can talk you through it even without formal training.

question: After any collision involving injury to another person, what are you legally required to do?
options: Nothing, if you believe it wasn't your fault
Stop, and provide your details (or report to police within 24 hours if you can't give them at the scene)
Only stop if the other party asks you to
Leave a note only if no one is around
explanation: Stopping and exchanging details — or reporting promptly if that's not possible at the scene — is a legal requirement, regardless of fault.

question: Why should uninjured people generally get out of a crashed vehicle on a busy road via the side away from traffic, if it's safe to do so?
options: It makes no difference which side is used
Stepping directly into a live traffic lane is extremely dangerous
It's only relevant for the driver, not passengers
This only applies on motorways
explanation: Exiting away from moving traffic, when it's safe to do so, avoids adding a second incident to the first.

question: When loading a car boot, where should the heaviest items generally be placed?
options: As high up and to the back as possible
Low down and, where possible, towards the front of the load area, spread evenly
It doesn't matter as long as everything fits
Always on the roof to save boot space
explanation: Keeping heavy items low and evenly distributed helps maintain the vehicle's stability and handling.

question: How does carrying a heavy load generally affect your vehicle's stopping distance?
options: It has no effect at all
It increases stopping distance, so extra following distance is needed
It always decreases stopping distance
It only affects steering, not braking
explanation: More weight means more momentum to stop, which increases the distance needed to brake safely — allow extra room accordingly.

question: Why should loads on a roof rack be properly secured?
options: It's just for tidiness
An insecure load could shift, fall onto the road or affect the vehicle's stability, creating a hazard for others
It's only a legal issue, not a safety one
Roof racks are always weight-limited so this isn't a real concern
explanation: A poorly secured roof load is a serious hazard, both to your own vehicle's handling and to other road users if it comes loose.

question: When towing a trailer or caravan, why might you need additional exterior mirrors?
options: They are just a legal formality with no practical benefit
A wide trailer or caravan can block your normal view to the rear, so extended mirrors help restore visibility
Standard mirrors are always sufficient regardless of trailer width
Extra mirrors are only needed for commercial vehicles
explanation: If the towed load is wider than the car, standard mirrors may not show you what's happening behind and to the sides — extended-arm mirrors compensate for this.

question: What is 'snaking' when towing a caravan or trailer?
options: A normal driving technique for cornering
A side-to-side oscillation of the trailer that can become dangerous if not corrected
A method of reversing a trailer
A term for overloading the tow vehicle
explanation: Snaking can be triggered by crosswinds, overtaking traffic, or incorrect loading — easing off the accelerator gently (without braking harshly) is the usual advice to help it settle.

question: Why should you avoid overloading a vehicle beyond its manufacturer's specified limits?
options: It only affects fuel costs
It can affect handling, braking, tyre wear and may be illegal, increasing the risk of an incident
Manufacturer limits are just general suggestions with no real consequence
It's only a concern for vans and lorries, not cars
explanation: Every vehicle has a maximum weight it's designed to carry safely — exceeding it can compromise handling and braking, and can also be against the law.

question: A load carried inside the car, such as loose shopping or tools, should be
options: left loose, since it's inside the car it can't be a hazard
secured or stowed so it can't move around, especially under heavy braking
placed on the parcel shelf regardless of size
piled up on the back seat without restraint
explanation: Unsecured items inside the cabin can become dangerous projectiles under heavy braking or in a collision.

question: If a load extends beyond the rear of your vehicle, what is generally required?
options: Nothing, as long as you can still see out of the rear window
It should be clearly marked, for example with a warning flag or light, especially in poor light
It's always illegal regardless of marking
Only the driver needs to be aware of it, not other road users
explanation: An overhanging load needs to be visible to other road users, particularly as light fades, to avoid a collision with something that isn't obviously part of the vehicle.

question: Why is it important that a load doesn't obscure your number plate or lights?
options: It's only a cosmetic issue
Obscured lights or plates reduce your visibility to others and can be both dangerous and illegal
Only the front lights matter for this
This only applies to commercial vehicles
explanation: Other road users rely on seeing your lights and identifying your vehicle — a load that blocks these creates a genuine safety risk.

question: How does towing a heavy trailer generally affect acceleration and the ability to join fast-moving traffic?
options: It has no meaningful effect
It typically reduces acceleration, so more care and a bigger gap are needed when joining traffic
It always improves acceleration due to extra momentum
It only affects deceleration, not acceleration
explanation: The extra weight behind you reduces how quickly you can speed up, so you'll need a larger gap when joining a busier road.

question: When carrying passengers along with luggage, what's important to check before setting off?
options: Nothing beyond having enough seats
That the vehicle isn't overloaded in total, and that all passengers can wear seatbelts properly, unobstructed by luggage
Only the driver's seatbelt needs checking
Luggage always takes priority over passenger comfort
explanation: Both the combined weight and making sure luggage doesn't block seatbelts or exits are part of loading a vehicle safely with passengers aboard.

question: Uneven loading, with most weight on one side of the vehicle, can cause
options: no noticeable difference in handling
the vehicle to pull to one side and handle unpredictably, especially when braking or cornering
